1212.title: How he compiled
1212.hook: a weaver, a leatherworker and a Sufi, side by side with the Gurus: how Guru Arjan chose what went into the book
1212.howItsDone: In the gurdwara, the hymns of the Gurus and of the bhagats, such as Kabir, Ravidas and Sheikh Farid, are read and sung from the same Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs bow to the whole as the Guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Arjan sang that he keeps no fast of one faith or the other, and serves the One alone. Your line was serving the one.

A stack of handwritten pages, gathered from many hands. Some hold the Gurus' hymns, copied and recopied in different towns, a word drifting here and there. Some hold songs by saints who were never Gurus: a weaver, a man who worked with hides, a Sufi from the Punjab. And tradition says some pages going around carried the Guru's name without the Guru's voice. Somebody has to sit with all of it and decide what goes into one book, and what stays out. Today, Guru Arjan is the editor.
screen: `A STACK OF PAGES, MANY HANDS.` → `SAINTS WHO WERE NEVER GURUS.` → `WHAT GOES IN, WHAT STAYS OUT?`

segments.voice: You've met the scribe, Bhai Gurdas, and the Gurus answering Farid; today, the editor's test. Tradition says Guru Arjan gathered the hymns of the Gurus before him, added his own, and dictated the volume to Bhai Gurdas, who wrote it out. The book became the Adi Granth, which later became the Guru Granth Sahib. So what was his test? Not where a singer was born, which faith he grew up in, or whether his trade was respected. The test was whether the hymn agreed with the Guru's teaching: the One, the Name, the turning away from ego. Look who passed. Kabir calls himself a weaver in his own verses. Ravidas names his people's work with hides and dead cattle, work his society looked down on, and sings that the learned now bow to him because of the Name. Sheikh Farid, a Sufi, has his saloks near the end of the Granth. These aren't footnotes; they're sung in the gurdwara, in the same ragas as the Gurus' hymns. And among Farid's saloks, a few verses are marked Mahala three and Mahala five: Guru Amar Das and Guru Arjan, answering. Where one of Farid's lines could be heard too harshly, a Guru's line sits beside it, turning it a little. So choosing carefully meant a wide welcome and a real conversation. The Guru didn't flatten the voices into one. He let them sing, and he answered. His question wasn't, is this person like me? It was, does this agree with the truth?
screen: `THE GURU DICTATES, BHAI GURDAS WRITES.` · `THE TEST: DOES IT AGREE?` · `A WEAVER, A LEATHERWORKER, A SUFI.` · `THE GURUS ANSWER FARID.` · then, large: `HE CHOSE CAREFULLY.`

segments.voice: Let the voices of your week pass by, a podcast, a parent, a teacher, a song, a friend's text, without judging them yet. Then ask the editor's question of each: does this agree with the person I'm trying to become? Keep the one that stands out, maybe from somewhere you didn't expect, and hold one thing it said.
How he compiled. Guru Arjan gathered many voices, Gurus and saints, and kept the ones that agreed with the Guru's teaching, whoever sang them. Today's word.
Your line: he chose carefully. A wide welcome, and one test. I'll be here tomorrow.

1213.title: Guru Arjan close
1213.hook: poet, builder, editor and martyr: four names for one life
1213.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Arjan on his martyrdom day with kirtan, readings of his hymns such as Sukhmani, and chhabeel, roadside stands serving cool sweetened water to anyone passing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Arjan the editor: a weaver, a leatherworker and a Sufi in the same book as the Gurus. Your line was he chose carefully.

Four job titles, one life: poet, builder, editor, martyr. On a résumé they'd look like four different people: one at a desk with a pen, one on a building site with mud on his hands, one sorting pages by lamplight, one standing firm when the powerful came for him. In Sikh memory they're all the fifth Guru, Guru Arjan. Today, a step back to look at the whole man, and ask what ties the four together.
screen: `POET. BUILDER. EDITOR. MARTYR.` → `FOUR PEOPLE ON A RÉSUMÉ.` → `ONE LIFE: THE FIFTH GURU.`

segments.voice: The poet first. Guru Arjan wrote the Bavan Akhri, the alphabet that ends in grace. He wrote Sukhmani, a name often explained as the jewel of peace, and read for comfort. He wrote tera keeaa meethaa laagai: what You do seems sweet to me. The builder. At Amritsar, around the pool his father began, the Harmandir Sahib rose. Tradition says it was built with doors on every side, open to anyone from any direction. He sang that the Lord Himself stood to finish the saints' work. The editor: Gurus and bhagats, chosen carefully, gathered into one volume. And the martyr. History records that he was arrested under the Mughal emperor Jahangir and died in Lahore. Sikh tradition remembers torture, and remembers him meeting it without bitterness; Gurdwara Dera Sahib in Lahore marks the place tradition gives for his death. In the telling, that sweet line comes back. So what ties the four together? Each time, he made a place for other people to stand. A song you can rest inside. A pool and a building you can walk into from any side. A book you can bow to and read. And an example of faith that held under the worst kind of pressure. He didn't build for himself. You met the chhabeel back on day one hundred fifty: on his martyrdom day, Sikhs set up stands by the road and hand cool, sweet water to anyone passing, whoever they are. A sweet drink for a stranger, in memory of a man who called God's will sweet.
screen: `THE POET: ALPHABET, PEACE, SWEETNESS.` · `THE BUILDER: DOORS ON EVERY SIDE.` · `THE MARTYR: LAHORE, WITHOUT BITTERNESS.` · `A PLACE FOR OTHERS TO STAND.` · then, large: `POET AND BUILDER.`

segments.voice: Look around your life for something other people stand in, a family meal, a kind group chat, a shelf at work everyone uses, a song you sing to a child, and choose one. Picture it a little more open, like a door on another side. Hold that picture, and if you pray, remember Waheguru on each breath in.
Guru Arjan close. Poet, builder, editor and martyr: one life spent making places, in words and in stone, for other people to stand. Today's word.
Your line: poet and builder. Words and walls, both built for someone else. Until tomorrow.

1214.title: Fearlessness, the ninth Guru's gift
1214.hook: not being scared, and not being scary: the ninth Guru holds both in one line
1214.howItsDone: The saloks of Guru Tegh Bahadur are read near the end of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs quote this verse on fearing no one and frightening no one when they speak of his life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Arjan whole: poet, builder, editor, martyr. Your line was poet and builder.

Which is harder: not being scared, or not being scary? It's easy to practice one and forget the other. Some people get brave, and on the way they get loud, sharp, a little frightening to the people around them. Others work so hard at being gentle that they never stand up to anything. The ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, puts both in one short verse near the very end of the Guru Granth Sahib. Today, the gift Sikhs remember him for: fearlessness, with two halves.
screen: `NOT SCARED, OR NOT SCARY?` → `BRAVE AND SHARP, OR GENTLE AND SILENT.` → `ONE SHORT VERSE, TWO HALVES.`

segments.voice: The verse is one of his saloks, paraphrased: one who frightens no one, and who fears no one else, listen, O my mind, says Nanak, call that one wise. The ninth Guru signs as Nanak, as the Gurus do in the Granth. Notice the order. Frightening no one comes first. Fearlessness here isn't a warrior's swagger. It starts with the people around you being safe with you. Now go back to the Mul Mantar, the root verse at the Granth's opening, and a word this path has met before. Among its words for the One are nirbhau and nirvair: without fear, and without enmity, side by side. The ninth Guru's salok takes those two qualities of God and sets them inside a human being. Without fear, you don't bow to threats. Without enmity, you don't make threats. They hold each other up. A lot of frightening comes from being frightened. The boss who shouts is sometimes afraid of looking weak. The kid who bullies is sometimes scared at home. And fear can make us small enough to stand by while others are frightened. Cut one root, and the other weakens. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Tegh Bahadur living this line to the end, standing firm under pressure, without hatred for those applying it. That story comes in a couple of days. For now, just the line.
screen: `FRIGHTEN NO ONE, FEAR NO ONE.` · `FRIGHTENING NO ONE COMES FIRST.` · `NIRBHAU AND NIRVAIR, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `FEAR MAKES PEOPLE FRIGHTENING.` · then, large: `NEITHER FEAR NOR FRIGHTEN.`

segments.voice: First, bring to mind one person who might be a little afraid of you, a child, someone who reports to you, a waiter, and on the breath out, soften toward them. Then bring to mind one thing you've been afraid to say or do, and on the breath in, let your back straighten. Go back and forth, soft toward them, steady toward it, and if you pray, rest in the One who is without fear and without enmity.
Fearlessness. In the ninth Guru's salok, the wise one frightens no one and fears no one, both halves together. Today's word.
Your line: neither fear nor frighten. Brave and gentle, both halves at once. See you tomorrow.

1215.title: Detachment in the home
1215.hook: why go searching in the forest? the ninth Guru finds the One in the house
1215.howItsDone: Sikhs follow the Gurus in living as householders, keeping family and work while remembering the Name, rather than renouncing the world; this hymn of Guru Tegh Bahadur is sung in kirtan on that theme.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ninth Guru's two-sided fearlessness. Your line was neither fear nor frighten.

Seven in the morning. Lunches half packed, a kettle starting to whistle, someone who can't find a shoe, a phone buzzing on the counter. In the back of the mind runs an old idea: the real spiritual life is elsewhere. On a mountain, in a forest, in a quiet room where no one asks where the shoe is. Guru Tegh Bahadur had a family: a wife, Mata Gujri, and a son who would become the tenth Guru. He had a household, a sangat, and plenty of people asking him for things. And he wrote a hymn that begins with a question about that forest.
screen: `SEVEN A.M., A LOST SHOE.` → `THE REAL LIFE IS ELSEWHERE?` → `A GURU WITH A FAMILY.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raga Dhanasri, paraphrased. Why go searching for Him in the forest? He dwells in all, always untouched, and He lives with you too. Then two pictures: like the fragrance that lives in a flower, like the reflection that lives in a mirror. So He dwells within; search inside, brother. Look closely. The fragrance is all through the flower, but you can't pick it out and hold it. The reflection is in the mirror, but the mirror isn't stained by it. Present, and untouched, at the same time. That's the hymn's word for the One: alepa, unstained, unclinging. And if the One can live in everything without clinging, a person can live in a house the same way. That's what detachment means here. It isn't leaving, or caring less about the people at the breakfast table. It's loving the home without being owned by it: packing the lunch with full attention, and not falling apart when the day goes sideways. Tradition says Guru Tegh Bahadur spent long stretches in quiet remembrance at Bakala before the Guruship came to him; back in year one, a trader found him there. But quiet didn't mean leaving his family. He stayed a householder, and the hymn points the same way. It doesn't scorn the forest. It says the search can begin at home. Held lightly, a home doesn't get smaller. It gets roomier, with space for the kettle, the lost shoe, and the One who, the Guru says, was there the whole time.
screen: `WHY SEARCH IN THE FOREST?` · `FRAGRANCE IN A FLOWER, A FACE IN A MIRROR.` · `PRESENT, AND UNTOUCHED.` · `A HOUSEHOLDER, NOT A HERMIT.` · then, large: `HOME, HELD LIGHTLY.`

segments.voice: Walk through your home in your mind, room by room, and in each one notice a person or a thing you love there, letting the love be full. Then, on the breath out, let it rest there without grasping, the way a mirror holds a face and keeps no stain. If you pray, remember Waheguru as present in each room.
Detachment in the home. Living fully with family and work, like fragrance in a flower, present everywhere and clinging to nothing. Today's word.
Your line: home, held lightly. Full love, and no stain. Go gently.

1216.title: Freedom of conscience
1216.hook: a thread the Gurus did not wear, and the ninth Guru gave his life for others' right to wear it
1216.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom with kirtan, readings of his hymns and gatherings at gurdwaras, including Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib in Delhi, and speak of him as a defender of the freedom of faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, detachment in the home: fragrance in a flower, a face in a mirror. Your line was home, held lightly.

A cotton thread, worn across the chest. For some Hindu families it's the janeu, the sacred thread, put on in a ceremony and worn for life. In a passage of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak declines that thread and asks instead for one spun from compassion and contentment, a thread that never breaks or burns. And yet the ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, is remembered for giving his life so that other people could keep wearing theirs. How do the two fit?
screen: `A COTTON THREAD ACROSS THE CHEST.` → `GURU NANAK DECLINES IT.` → `THE NINTH GURU DIES FOR IT.`

segments.voice: You've met both halves before: the boy Nanak and the thread, and the pandits arriving at Anandpur. Here's the story as Sikh tradition tells it. A group of Kashmiri Pandits, Hindu scholars, came to Guru Tegh Bahadur at Anandpur. The Mughal authorities were pressing them to give up their faith and convert. Tradition says the Guru's young son, the future tenth Guru, was there, and said such a moment needed someone great to stand up. The Guru told the Pandits to send word to the emperor: if he converts, we will too. Then he went to Delhi. He was arrested and, refusing to give up his faith, he was executed in the city, at a spot Sikhs now mark with Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib. Later, a work attributed to the tenth Guru, the Bachittar Natak, sums it up, paraphrased: he protected their forehead mark and their sacred thread; he gave his head, but not his resolve. Hold that next to Guru Nanak's hymn. Guru Nanak had set the thread aside; his path had its own way. And the ninth Guru died for the right of people to keep a way that wasn't his. That's freedom of conscience, made concrete: not my faith, my right, but their faith, their right. The pressure came from the power of a state, not from the faith of ordinary neighbors. In Sikh memory, this is a stand against force, not against any people or religion. The Guru's answer wasn't to force anyone back. It was to stand between the weak and the strong, and not move.
screen: `THE PANDITS COME TO ANANDPUR.` · `THE GURU GOES TO DELHI.` · `HE GAVE HIS HEAD, NOT HIS RESOLVE.` · `A WAY THAT WASN'T HIS.` · then, large: `THEIR FAITH, THEIR RIGHT.`

segments.voice: Think of someone whose way of believing, praying or living differs from yours, a coworker who fasts, a neighbor who wears something you don't, a relative who left a tradition or joined one, and hold them in mind with respect. Then notice where their freedom might be squeezed by a joke or a schedule that ignores their holy day, and find one small way to make room. If you pray, remember Waheguru on each breath.
Freedom of conscience. The ninth Guru gave his life for the right of others to keep a faith that wasn't his own. Today's word.

1217.hook: a carpenter's bubble, and a hymn about one who sees gold and clay the same
1217.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns, such as this one in Raga Sorath, in kirtan, and his saloks on meeting pleasure and pain alike are read near the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, freedom of conscience: the ninth Guru went to Delhi for people whose thread he didn't wear. Your line was their faith, their right.

A carpenter's level is a simple tool: a little tube of liquid with one bubble trapped inside. Tilt the board one way and the bubble runs off. Tilt it the other way and it runs off again. Only when the board is true does the bubble sit still, right between the two lines. Plenty of days feel like a board tipped back and forth. Good news, and the bubble runs. Bad news, and it runs the other way. Guru Tegh Bahadur wrote a hymn about a person whose bubble stays in the middle.
screen: `A TUBE, ONE BUBBLE.` → `TILT, AND IT RUNS.` → `A PERSON WHO STAYS LEVEL.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raga Sorath, paraphrased. The one who, in pain, does not take pain as pain. Who has no clinging to pleasure, and no fear. Who looks on gold as clay. Who is moved neither by slander nor by praise, and is free of greed, attachment and pride. Who stays the same in joy and sorrow, in honor and dishonor. In that one, the hymn says, the Lord lives; such a person blends with the Lord like water into water. Notice what the hymn doesn't say. It doesn't say the level person feels nothing, or that pain isn't real. It keeps returning to pairs: pain and pleasure, praise and slander, gold and clay. The point isn't escaping one side. It's not being thrown by either. A raise and a rejection both meet the same steady person. And this wasn't theory for the man who wrote it. His life ended in Delhi, and Sikh tradition remembers him meeting it calmly. A short salok of his says the same in fewer words: the one untouched by pleasure and pain, by greed, attachment and pride, is the very image of the Lord. A normal day asks nothing like that, but the bubble still runs: a text that stings, a compliment that goes to your head. Notice the tilt, and let the bubble come back. And if pain right now is more than you can carry, staying level never means staying alone: in the US, call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.
screen: `IN PAIN, NOT TAKING PAIN AS PAIN.` · `GOLD AND CLAY, PRAISE AND SLANDER.` · `WATER BLENDING INTO WATER.` · `NOT THROWN BY EITHER SIDE.` · then, large: `LEVEL.`

segments.voice: Notice the mood you're in right now and name it plainly, tired, happy, worried, flat, without pushing it away or feeding it. Picture the bubble in the level, and with each breath out let it settle a little nearer the middle, noticing whatever pulls it up or down. If you pray, rest in Waheguru on each breath.
Suffering calmly. The ninth Guru's hymn praises one who meets pain and pleasure, praise and slander, gold and clay the same, and stays level. Today's word.
Your line: level. Not numb, just not thrown, whichever way the board tips. Until tomorrow.

1218.title: The traveler's hymns
1218.hook: a Guru on the road east, and a hymn that asks the mind to take shelter
1218.howItsDone: Gurdwaras stand at places tradition links to Guru Tegh Bahadur's journeys, including Patna Sahib, and Sikhs sing his hymns in kirtan; some Sikhs also recite or listen to gurbani while traveling.

segments.voice: Yesterday, suffering calmly, and a carpenter's bubble in the level. Your line was level.

Dust on the road. A river to cross by boat, then another. Days of walking and riding, nights in the homes of strangers who become sangat by morning. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Tegh Bahadur as a traveler, journeying east toward Bengal and Assam, visiting Sikhs and meeting seekers along the way. Tradition says his son, the future tenth Guru, was born at Patna while he was away on those journeys. A Guru on the road, far from home. And some of his hymns, tradition says, belong to those roads.
screen: `DUST, RIVERS, STRANGERS' HOMES.` → `EAST, TOWARD BENGAL AND ASSAM.` → `HYMNS FROM THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: First, an honest thing. The Guru Granth Sahib arranges his hymns by raga, by musical mode, not by place. There's no map beside each one, so when people link a hymn to a journey, that's tradition and memory, not a label in the book. But listen to what his hymns sound like, and the road is there. One, in Raga Sorath, paraphrased, begins: O mind, take the shelter of the Lord's Name; remembering it, bad thinking is destroyed, and the highest state is reached. Shelter: in Gurmukhi, ot. On a long road you don't need a palace; you need somewhere to stand out of the rain. And notice who the hymn talks to. Not the crowd, not a king. O mind. It turns to the one companion who comes on every journey, the voice in your own head, often the only one listening. So a traveler's hymn is a hymn you can carry: no building required, no instrument, no gathering. Just a line, and a mind to say it to. That's prayer on the road. This week has traveled too: Guru Arjan the editor and his whole life, then the ninth Guru's fearlessness, a home held lightly, their faith, their right, and a level heart. Different roads, one shelter.
screen: `ARRANGED BY RAGA, NOT BY PLACE.` · `O MIND, TAKE SHELTER.` · `A HYMN YOU CAN CARRY.` · `A WEEK ON THE ROAD.` · then, large: `PRAYER ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Ride your next trip in your mind, even a short one, the drive to work, the bus, the walk to the store, and pick one spot on the route to be your shelter: a light, a corner, a bridge. Picture reaching it and speaking to your own mind for one breath. If you pray, the word can be Waheguru; if you don't, simply: here, now.
The traveler's hymns. Guru Tegh Bahadur journeyed east, and his hymns speak to the mind, offering a shelter you can carry anywhere. Today's word.
Your line: prayer on the road. Ot, a shelter that travels with you. That's today, done.
